name.text: 26.2 Circle Theorems - Cyclic Quadrilaterals, Alternate Segment Theory

questiontext.text:
\(A, B, C, D\) are points on a circle, centre \(O\).
There is a tangent to the circle at \(A\).

truefeedback.text:
Here is a worked solution:

In a cyclic quadrilateral, the opposite angles have a sum of \(180^\circ\).

We can show this using the fact that an angle formed at the centre of a sector is twice the angle formed at the circumference.

[[jsxgraph height="360px" width="400px"]] var angBCA = {#angBCA#}; var angADC = {#angADC#}; JXG.Options.text.useMathJax=true; var board = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, { boundingBox:[-5,4,5,-4], showCopyright:false, showNavigation:false, keepaspectratio:true }); var pointStyle = { fixed:true, highlight:false, showInfoBox:false, withLabel:true, label:{ fixed:true, highlight:false, fontSize:15, useMathJax:true, parse:false } }; pointStyle.name = " "; var pO = board.create("point", [0,0], pointStyle); var circle = board.create("circle", [3, pO], { fixed:true, highlight:false, strokeColor:"black" }); board.create("segment", [[-4,-3], [4,-3]], { fixed:true, highlight:false, strokeColor:"black" }); pointStyle.name = "\\(A\\)"; pointStyle.label.offset = [5,-15]; var pA = board.create("glider", [0, -3, circle], pointStyle); var lineAB = board.create("line", [ pA, [Math.cos(angBCA*Math.PI/180), Math.sin(angBCA*Math.PI/180)-3] ], {visible:false}); pointStyle.name = "\\(B\\)"; pointStyle.label.offset = [10,5]; var pB = board.create("intersection", [circle, lineAB], pointStyle); var lineBC = board.create("line", [ pB, [pB.X()-Math.cos((180-angADC-angBCA)*Math.PI/180), pB.Y()+Math.sin((180-angADC-angBCA)*Math.PI/180)] ], {visible:false}); pointStyle.name = "\\(C\\)"; pointStyle.label.offset = [-20,10]; var pC = board.create("intersection", [circle, lineBC], pointStyle); pointStyle.name = "\\(D\\)"; pointStyle.label.offset = [-25,5]; var pD = board.create("glider", [-3, 0, circle], pointStyle); board.create("polygon", [pA, pB, pC, pD], { fixed:true, highlight:false, fillColor:"none", borders:{ fixed:true, highlight:false, strokeColor:"blue", strokeWidth:2 } }); board.create("segment", [pO, pA], { fixed:true, highlight:false, dash:2 }); board.create("segment", [pO, pC], { fixed:true, highlight:false, dash:2 }); var angStyle = { highlight:false, withLabel:false, radius:0.75 }; angStyle.fillColor = "red"; angStyle.strokeColor = "red"; board.create("angle", [pC, pO, pA], angStyle); angStyle.fillColor = "orange"; angStyle.strokeColor = "orange"; board.create("angle", [pC, pB, pA], angStyle); angStyle.fillColor = "blue"; angStyle.strokeColor = "blue"; board.create("angle", [pA, pO, pC], angStyle); angStyle.fillColor = "green"; angStyle.strokeColor = "green"; board.create("angle", [pA, pD, pC], angStyle); [[/jsxgraph]]

Summing the angles at the centre of the circle: \(\theta_R + \theta_B = 360^\circ\)

Relating these to the angles at the circumference: \(\theta_R = 2\theta_Y\) and \(\theta_B = 2\theta_G\)

Putting these together: \(2\theta_Y + 2\theta_G = 360^\circ\)

Therefore: \(\theta_Y + \theta_G = 180^\circ\)

The sum of the opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral is 180 degrees.

The green angles can be related using the Alternate Segment Theorem.
So, \(BCA = {@angBCA@}^\circ\)

The red and orange angles can be related using the circle theorem form part (a).
So, \(ABC = 180 - {@angADC@} = {@180-angADC@}^\circ\)

Since there are \(180^\circ\) in a triangle, \(CAB + {@angBCA@} + {@180-angADC@} = 180^\circ\)
Therefore, \(CAB = {@angADC-angBCA@}^\circ\)
